flagged.title: Early modern crime: heresy, treason and witchcraft
flagged.reason: The audio erroneously names the monarch behind the 1604 Witchcraft Act as 'James the Third' instead of James I, which is a key historical figure on the GCSE specification.

mark_affecting.video_says: and James the Third increased the penalties again in 1604.
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Further Acts in 1563 (under Elizabeth I) and 1604 (under James I) tightened the law and increased the penalties.

flagged.title: The Gunpowder Plot and the start of the Bloody Code
flagged.reason: The video includes the inaccurate claim that two-thirds of capital property offenders had sentences commuted to transportation by 1700 (F19).

mark_affecting.quote: Even so, by 1700, about two-thirds of those sentenced to death for property crimes had their sentences commuted to transportation.

flagged.title: Modern policing, the death penalty and the Bentley case
flagged.reason: The video and slide at 02:10–02:37 teach the incorrect date of 1986 for the conviction of Colin Pitchfork (the first DNA conviction), which occurred in 1988.

mark_affecting.quote: in 1986, Colin Pitchfork became the first person in the entire world to be convicted using DNA evidence

flagged.title: Investigating the Ripper: detection, sources and the press
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims that Catherine Eddowes was photographed at the crime scene in Mitre Square, whereas she was only photographed at the mortuary and Mary Jane Kelly at Miller's Court was the sole in-situ crime scene photograph.

mark_affecting.quote: In fact, Catherine Eddowes' body in Mitre Square was photographed by the City of London Police, which was actually a first for a Met investigation
